newsitem.title: USA: Toyota, Honda say not planning to cut U.S. exports.
newsitem.headline: Toyota, Honda say not planning to cut U.S. exports.

text.p: Toyota Motor Corp and Honda Motor Co Ltd officials in the United States said Wednesday they know of no planned reductions in exports to the United States by the Japanese automakers.
A published report from the Nihon Keizai Shimbun newspaper said Wednesday Toyota and Honda plan to cut their U.S. shipments by a combined 100,000 units, bringing their 1997 exports to the 1996 level.
Officials from Detroit's Big Three have complained the weak yen is making it more profitable for Japanese automakers to export vehicles to the United States and unfairly grab market share.
"Nothing has changed as far as I can determine," said Honda spokesman Andrew Boyd.
Honda expects to export 200,000 units to the United States in 1997, up from about 151,000 for 1996. The CR-V, a popular small sport/utility vehicle, will account for much of the increase, he said.

Toyota spokesman Tim Andree said Toyota still expects its total 1997 U.S. shipments to be flat or slightly down from the 432,000 units exported in both 1996 and 1995."We don't expect a significant deviation from that level," he said.

Both Honda and Toyota, Japan's largest automaker, have been relying on shipments from Japan to supplement U.S. production in order to meet strong demand for popular car and small sport/utility vehicles.

Andree at Toyota said first quarter exports to the U.S. were 119,127 units, an increase of 29 percent from a year ago. Accounting for the increase were shipments of the Camry sedan, and 4Runner and RAV4 sport/utility vehicles.

U.S. government figures released Wednesay showed the U.S. trade deficit with Japan grew 8.3 percent in March to a total of $4.6 billion. Auto industry officials said the figures show the weak yen is continuing to hurt domestic automakers.

"The March trade figures confirm the trend that America's Car companies have been warning about for months: despite the strong U.S. economy, the excessively weak yen is causing a worsening of the trade deficit with Japan," Andrew Card, president of the American Automobile Manufacturer's Association, said in a statement.
